title: Database Indexing Handbook: Pages, B+ Trees and Index Costs
summary: Quick revision notes on how databases store rows in pages and records, how primary, secondary, clustered and non-clustered indexes work, how B+ trees and hash indexes find rows, and what indexes cost on writes.

chapters.title: Pages and Records: Storage Basics
points: Page: fixed-size disk block (often 4-16 KB; 8 KB in PostgreSQL, 16 KB in InnoDB) and the smallest unit read or written by the DB, so one row lookup reads a whole page
Record (row) lives in a slot inside a page; a slot directory maps slot number to byte offset, so a record ID is (page number, slot number)
Heap file: pages in no particular order, so finding a row without an index means a full scan of every page
Fixed-length records give a simple offset calculation; variable-length records (VARCHAR) need the slot directory and can overflow into extra pages
Cost model: query speed is measured in page I/Os, not rows, so fewer pages touched means a faster query

chapters.title: Primary vs Secondary and Clustered vs Non-Clustered
points: Primary index is built on the primary key (unique, not null); a secondary index is built on any other column and can be non-unique
Clustered index: the table rows are physically stored in index key order in the leaf pages, so there is only one per table
Non-clustered index: leaf entries hold the key plus a pointer to the row (a record ID in the heap, or the primary key in InnoDB)
InnoDB secondary lookup does two traversals: the secondary index to get the primary key, then the clustered index to get the row
Range scans on the clustered key read adjacent pages sequentially, while the same range on a non-clustered index causes random row fetches

chapters.title: B+ Trees: The Default Index Structure
points: B+ tree: balanced tree where internal nodes hold only keys and child pointers, and all data or row pointers sit in the leaf level
Leaves are linked in a doubly linked list, so range queries find the start key and then walk the leaves sideways
Each node is one page with a high fan-out (hundreds of children), so a tree over millions of rows is only 3-4 levels deep
Lookup cost is O(log_f N) page reads, where f is the fan-out; for example, 3 levels is 3 page I/Os, with the root usually cached
Insert into a full leaf splits it in two and pushes a separator key up to the parent, which can cascade up to the root; this keeps the tree balanced
Composite index (a,b,c) follows the leftmost-prefix rule: it serves filters on a, a+b, or a+b+c, but not b alone

chapters.title: Hash Indexes vs B+ Trees
points: Hash index applies a hash function to the key to pick a bucket, giving O(1) average equality lookup (WHERE id = 5)
Hash indexes cannot serve range queries, ORDER BY or prefix matches, because hashing destroys key order
Collisions are handled by chaining in the bucket or by overflow pages; too many collisions degrade lookups toward O(n)
Comparison: B+ tree supports =, <, >, BETWEEN, ORDER BY and LIKE 'abc%' at O(log N); hash supports only = but is faster for it
Practice: MySQL InnoDB has an adaptive hash index built automatically in memory, and PostgreSQL has CREATE INDEX ... USING hash; B+ tree is the default in both

chapters.title: Index Maintenance Cost, Mistakes and Cheat Sheet
points: Every INSERT or DELETE updates the table plus every index on it, so 5 indexes means about 6 structures written per row
UPDATE on an indexed column moves the entry in that index, while updating an unindexed column leaves the indexes untouched
Mistake: indexing every column, which slows writes, wastes memory and disk, and lets the planner pick wrong; index only columns used in WHERE, JOIN and ORDER BY
Mistake: indexing low-cardinality columns such as boolean or gender, where the planner usually prefers a full scan anyway
Mistake: random keys such as UUIDv4 as a clustered key cause page splits and fragmentation, while sequential keys append to the last page
Cheat sheet: equality only means hash; range or sort means B+ tree; one clustered index per table; leftmost prefix for composite; read-heavy tables get more indexes, write-heavy tables get fewer
